# Genomics {#sec-genomics}

::: {.callout-note title="From the exam description"}
Methods for sequencing, algorithms for assembly, gene predictions, etc.
:::

## Introduction

Genomics begins with reading DNA. Sanger's chain-termination method
[@sanger1977], automated with fluorescent dyes [@smith1986], produced
reads of up to about 1,000 bases. It was used for the first genomes,
including the human genome. From 2005, "next-generation" methods made
sequencing massively parallel: 454 pyrosequencing
[@ronaghi1998; @margulies2005] and above all Illumina sequencing by
synthesis [@bentley2008]. This reduced costs by many orders of magnitude,
but produced short reads (100–300 bp). Third-generation single-molecule
technologies, PacBio and Oxford Nanopore, produce reads that are tens of
kilobases or longer [@jain2018]. At first these reads had high error
rates. PacBio HiFi reads are now both long and accurate [@goodwin2016].

There are two main ways to use reads. **De novo assembly** reconstructs a
genome without a reference. The main difficulty is repeats that are
longer than the reads. Early assemblers used the overlap–layout–consensus
paradigm [@anson1999; @myers2000], later formalised as the string graph
[@myers2005]. For millions of short reads, computing all pairwise
overlaps is too expensive. De Bruijn graph assemblers instead break reads
into *k*-mers and look for an Eulerian path through the graph
[@pevzner2001; @zerbino2008; @compeau2011]. Long accurate reads have
brought the field back to overlap-based methods. They now make possible
haplotype-resolved [@cheng2021] and complete, telomere-to-telomere
assemblies [@nurk2022]. Assemblies are judged by contiguity (N50), by
completeness (e.g. how many conserved single-copy genes are found) and
by comparison between assemblers [@bradnam2013].

**Resequencing** maps reads to a reference genome. Aligners for short
reads index the reference with the Burrows–Wheeler transform and FM-index,
which allow exact matches to be found in memory proportional to the
genome size and in time independent of it [@langmead2009; @li2009].
minimap2 uses minimizer seeds and chaining for long reads [@li2018].
Each alignment is given a mapping quality, which expresses the
uncertainty in reads from repetitive regions. **Variant calling** then
combines evidence from many reads with base and mapping qualities in a
probabilistic model to compute genotype likelihoods
[@marth1999; @li2008; @li2011; @depristo2011]. More recently,
deep-learning callers treat the problem as image classification
[@poplin2018].

A genome sequence is only useful once its genes are found. In
prokaryotes, gene finding is relatively easy because genes are dense and
lack introns. HMM-based tools such as GeneMark reach high accuracy
[@lukashin1998]. In eukaryotes, genes are split into exons separated by
introns that can be very long. Ab initio predictors such as GENSCAN model
the gene structure with generalised HMMs [@burge1997]. Modern annotation
pipelines combine such predictions with evidence from RNA-seq and protein
alignments.

## Key concepts

- Sequencing technologies: Sanger, pyrosequencing/454, Illumina (sequencing by synthesis), PacBio (HiFi), Oxford Nanopore; read lengths, error profiles, cost
- Shotgun sequencing; coverage (Lander–Waterman); paired-end and mate-pair reads
- Assembly paradigms: overlap–layout–consensus, string graphs, de Bruijn graphs; repeats as the central problem; scaffolding
- Assembly quality: N50, BUSCO, Assemblathon; telomere-to-telomere assemblies; haplotype-resolved assembly
- Read mapping: hashing/seeds vs. Burrows–Wheeler/FM-index (Bowtie, BWA), long-read mapping (minimap2); mapping quality
- Variant calling: SNPs, indels, structural variants; genotype likelihoods; GATK; deep-learning callers
- Gene prediction: ab initio (HMM-based: GeneMark, GENSCAN), homology- and RNA-seq-based evidence; prokaryotic vs. eukaryotic gene finding
- Metagenomics (overview)

## Key papers

::: {.callout-tip}
★ = mandatory in earlier reading lists.
:::

### Reviews — start here

- @goodwin2016 — ten years of next-generation sequencing technologies.
- @compeau2011 — how to apply de Bruijn graphs to genome assembly.

### Sequencing technologies

- @sanger1977 — chain-terminating sequencing.
- @smith1986 — fluorescence detection in automated sequencing.
- @ronaghi1998 — pyrosequencing.
- @margulies2005 — 454 sequencing in picolitre reactors.
- @bentley2008 — Illumina reversible-terminator chemistry.
- @jain2018 — nanopore sequencing of a human genome with ultra-long reads.

### Genome assembly

- @anson1999 — algorithms for whole-genome shotgun sequencing.
- @myers2000 — whole-genome assembly of *Drosophila*.
- @pevzner2001 — an Eulerian path approach to assembly.
- ★ @myers2005 — the fragment assembly string graph.
- @zerbino2008 — Velvet: de Bruijn graph assembly of short reads.
- @bradnam2013 — Assemblathon 2: evaluating assemblers.
- @cheng2021 — hifiasm: haplotype-resolved assembly from HiFi reads.
- @nurk2022 — the complete (telomere-to-telomere) human genome.

### Read mapping and variant calling

- ★ @langmead2009 — Bowtie: ultrafast BWT-based alignment.
- @li2009 — BWA.
- @li2018 — minimap2.
- @li2008 — mapping quality and variant calling (MAQ).
- @marth1999 — a general approach to SNP discovery.
- @li2011 — a statistical framework for SNP calling.
- @depristo2011 — GATK: variation discovery and genotyping.
- @poplin2018 — DeepVariant: variant calling with a deep neural network.

### Gene prediction

- @burge1997 — GENSCAN: gene structure prediction in human genomic DNA.
- ★ @lukashin1998 — GeneMark.hmm.
